title: 49 minutes of terror and tragedy in Toronto
article: The man slain by a police sharpshooter outside Toronto's packed Union Station yesterday after attacking his wife and holding a woman hostage was under a restraining order to stay away from his family and from weapons.
Sugston Anthony Brookes had spent two months in jail this summer for assaulting his wife and daughter. A month ago, Marlene Brookes filed for divorce.
Yesterday, shortly after 8 a.m., he confronted Mrs. Brookes as she went to work at Preeners Cleaners in the concourse level of the downtown Toronto-Dominion Centre, where she makes $350 a week.
Mr. Brookes fired shots in his wife's direction with a sawed-off rifle, but did not hit her. He then beat her, as witnesses ran for cover and called 911.
Minutes later, he left the TD Centre. When police spotted him a block south, outside Union Station, he had grabbed a hostage, a woman identified by CTV News as Nicole Regis.
Forty minutes later, a police sniper's bullet entered his head as hundreds of commuters and workers watched from behind police lines and at office tower windows. His blood stained the sidewalk.

What finished as a violent public spectacle had begun as an escalating series of domestic assaults that for years went mostly unnoticed behind the walls of the suburban family home in Ajax, east of Toronto, according to the divorce papers.
Marlene Brookes moved out of the house in March, taking her two children with her. In May, she had her husband successfully prosecuted for assaulting her and her daughter.

On July 29, she marked his release from jail by filing the divorce papers alleging he had frittered away nearly $200,000, fathered three children out of wedlock, and carried out attacks with knives, fireplace pokers, and gas cans.
This spring, courts forbade Mr. Brookes to carry any sort of weapons and to come into any contact with his wife and children.
The man who would die as a hostage-taker lived most of his life as a simple family man in the suburbs, working at the Hudson's Bay Co. as he tried to pay off a substantial mortgage.

Neighbours on Ajax's Marshall Crescent, where the Brookeses' grey brick home has a newly trimmed lawn and a basketball net hanging from the garage, remember him as a generous father who manned a barbecue at a block party just this past Canada Day.
He talked with other adults until 3 a.m., but no one really wanted to ask him why his wife and children had moved away.
"I hope they don't make him out to be some kind of monster," neighbour Cindy Christodoulou said yesterday.
"He wasn't like that at all: He was a good man."
The Brookeses' mortgage broker, Scott Lindsey, said his client was "absolutely a normal, cordial person."
The family's life took a turn for the worse when Mr. Brookes was fired from his job at the Bay in 2001 after 23 years, according to the divorce papers.
He received a severance payment of more than $100,000, and took a job delivering The Globe and Mail for $420 weekly.
He began his day yesterday as he usually did, rising before dawn to deliver 72 papers.
Marlene Brookes now says, in the divorce papers, that her relationship with her husband, though it seemed happy to neighbours, "has been characterized by physical violence."
"Until recently she did not report these incidents to the police and, when she attended the hospital, she lied about the source of injuries," the documents say.
"He has held a knife to her throat and he has punched her and choked her, and he has carried gasoline into the... house and threatened to burn it down."
It was not only his wife who bore the brunt of his frustration, the documents allege. Once, Mr. Brookes "drove through Ajax with an iron poker from the parties' fireplace" looking for his son.
He is said to have hit his teenaged daughter "until her eye turned black and blue."
The violence seems to have escalated this year.
The divorce documents say that in February, Mr. Brookes pushed his wife down the stairs, held a knife to her head, and, using an expletive, said that he was going to cut her throat.

Marlene Brookes also accuses her husband of fathering another child with a Toronto woman and two more Canadian-born children with a woman who now lives in the West Indies, all during the course of their marriage.

In March, police in suburban Durham Region, which lies east of Toronto and where people still recall the failure of the criminal-justice system to protect Gillian Hadley from a deranged and homicidal husband four years ago, arrested Mr. Brookes for assault, assault with a weapon, and uttering death threats against members of his family.
But his sentence was short. In May, after pleading guilty and serving 26 days awaiting trial, he was sentenced to the equivalent of a month in jail.
A restraining order forbade him to come within 100 metres of his wife, children, or any of their schools or workplaces or to carry any weapons for 10 years.
Besides delivering papers, Mr. Brookes had found another job and had gotten his newspaper-delivery boss to keep the job open for him while he went to jail.
He even negotiated an extra $400 advance this past weekend.
Yesterday, his father, Vincent Brookes, turned on the television to see his son take a woman hostage.
"We couldn't believe it when we saw it on the news," he said. "We called the police to confirm it was him, and they said yes."
The elder Mr. Brookes said he had last spoken to his son on the weekend. He said he hasn't had any contact with his grandchildren since his son's marriage broke up.
Sitting in his car outside his home in suburban Oshawa, his eyes red from crying, Mr. Brookes said: "This is terrible, that's for sure."
